passages.t: Benjamin, and the family of Saul
passages.happening:
Benjamin's sons are named (verses 1-5), and then clusters of families tied to places: Geba, Moab, Ono and Lod, Aijalon, Jerusalem and Gibeon (verses 6-32). Some Benjaminites drive out the people of Gath (verse 13), and some live ‘in Jerusalem’ (verse 28).

The chapter ends with Saul's family. ‘Ner was the father of Kish, Kish was the father of Saul, and Saul was the father of Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal’ (verse 33). ‘The son of Jonathan: Merib-baal’ (verse 34). The line runs on for many generations, down to the sons of Ulam, who ‘were mighty men of valor, archers, and they had many sons and grandsons’ (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Benjamin gets a whole chapter for two reasons. With Judah and Levi it formed the core of the kingdom of Judah after the north broke away, and Benjaminites were among those who came home from exile. And Benjamin was the tribe of Saul, whose death opens David's story in chapter 10.

Benjamin's land was small but strategic, between Judah and Ephraim just north of Jerusalem, which sat on the border. Ono and Lod appear among the towns resettled after the exile. Ehud in verse 6 may be the left-handed judge of Judges, a Benjaminite. Benjaminite fighters were famous; their slingers and archers appear again when they come over to David.

Saul's family is set before the reader without comment. His sons Jonathan, Malchishua and Abinadab died with him on Mount Gilboa. Esh-baal is the son called Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel, who reigned briefly over the north. Merib-baal is Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, lame from childhood, to whom David showed kindness for Jonathan's sake. Saul's line did not die with him. The house that lost the throne was not wiped out. These verses are repeated in 9:35-44, where they lead straight into Saul's death, like a hinge between the lists and the story.
passages.later: David told Jonathan's son, ‘surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan’ (2 Samuel 9:7). Paul, who bore Saul's name, wrote that he was ‘of the tribe of Benjamin’ (Philippians 3:5).
passages.hard:
Why did Saul's family have names containing Baal, and why are they different in Samuel?

The Hebrew word baal is an ordinary noun meaning owner, lord or husband, and it was also the title of the leading Canaanite god. Many scholars think that in Saul's day Israelites could use baal as a title for the LORD, so that Esh-baal meant something like man of the lord, with no intent to honor the Canaanite god. Others think the names show that Canaanite religion had touched even Saul's household. Later, when the prophets were fighting the worship of Baal, the word became so tainted that writers avoided it. The books of Samuel, as they have come down, replace baal with bosheth, shame, giving Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth. Whether the authors of Samuel or later copyists made the change is debated. Chronicles keeps the older forms, which suggests the Chronicler drew on records, or a text of Samuel, from before the change.
passages.asks: Saul's house lost the throne and still went on for generations. Ask what it means that God does not erase families who have fallen. And ask whom you could treat as David treated Jonathan's son.
